14	// dlqPublishTimeout bounds one dead-letter PublishMsg. The consume context has
15	// no deadline, and PublishMsg waits for the PubAck indefinitely; without a
16	// bound a NATS blip would hang the handler (and, since a one-in-flight consumer
17	// keeps a slot occupied, stall the consumer) instead of failing the capture
18	// loudly.
19	const dlqPublishTimeout = 15 * time.Second

21	// DLQ provenance headers added to the captured copy so a replay tool (or a
22	// human) can see why and from where a message was dead-lettered.
23	//
24	// They divide into two groups, and the division is the whole contract. ORIGIN
25	// headers describe where the message ultimately came from and are WRITE-ONCE: a
26	// capture fills one in only if it is not already there, so re-capturing a message
27	// — whether the same original after a failed Ack, or a DLQ record a replay tool
28	// has given up on — never overwrites the first hop's answer. PER-HOP headers
29	// describe the capture that just happened and are written fresh every time.
30	const (
31		// DLQReasonHeader is per-hop: why THIS capture gave up.
32		DLQReasonHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Reason"
33		// DLQDeliveredHeader is per-hop: the delivery count this capture saw.
34		DLQDeliveredHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Delivered"
35		// DLQHopsHeader counts captures. The library derives it by incrementing
36		// whatever it found, so it is 1 on a first capture and tells a reader that
37		// earlier hops exist — their reasons are not in these headers, because reason
38		// is per-hop.
39		DLQHopsHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Hops"
40	
41		// DLQOriginHeader is write-once: the subject the message was first published
42		// to.
43		DLQOriginHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Subject"
44		// DLQStreamSeqHeader is write-once: the stream sequence the message was first
45		// stored at.
46		DLQStreamSeqHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Stream-Seq"
47		// DLQOriginStreamHeader is write-once: the stream the message was first stored
48		// on.
49		DLQOriginStreamHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Stream"
50		// DLQOriginDomainHeader is write-once: the JetStream domain that stream was
51		// in, empty outside a domain. Two deployments can hold same-named streams, so
52		// replay tooling needs it to tell their records apart.
53		DLQOriginDomainHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Domain"
54		// DLQOriginTimestampHeader is write-once: when the message was first stored, as
55		// RFC3339 with nanoseconds.
56		//
57		// It is the field that distinguishes two incarnations of one stream, since a
58		// recreated stream restarts its sequence numbering. Origin stream, sequence,
59		// domain and timestamp together identify a stored message, which is what
60		// replay-side dedupe should key on — see [DeadLetter] on why capture no longer
61		// dedupes at all.
62		DLQOriginTimestampHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Timestamp"
63		// DLQOriginMsgIDHeader is write-once: the Nats-Msg-Id the message carried when
64		// it was first captured, which is the publisher's own dedupe key and the thing
65		// a replay tool needs to restore it upstream. It cannot stay under its own name
66		// — see [DeadLetter] on the header policy.
67		DLQOriginMsgIDHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Msg-Id"
68		// DLQOriginRecordedHeader marks the origin block as filled in, and is what makes
69		// write-once mean write-once.
70		//
71		// Field-by-field absence cannot carry that fact, because absence is ambiguous:

73		// and one captured with no metadata at all has no origin stream, sequence or
74		// store time either. Reading those absences as "not yet recorded" let a LATER
75		// hop fill them in from itself — writing its own domain, or the DLQ stream it

77		// which is worse than none.
78		//
79		// So the block is written exactly once, as a block. When this marker is present
80		// every origin field is carried through as-is and none is derived, whatever is
81		// or is not there: an absent field means the hop that recorded the origin had
82		// nothing to record for it, and no later hop is entitled to a better answer.
83		DLQOriginRecordedHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Recorded"

86		// NOT a retention rule: an inbound header merely because it carries this prefix
87		// is dropped, and only the specific origin headers above are carried forward.
88		// See [DeadLetter].
89		DLQHeaderPrefix = "Nats-Dlq-"
90	)

92	// dlqCarriedProvenance are the origin headers a capture preserves from the
93	// message it is capturing, rather than deriving. They are the write-once set: a
94	// value already present describes an earlier hop and is the answer to keep.
95	//
96	// It is a closed list of keys this package defines, deliberately, rather than the
97	// whole [DLQHeaderPrefix]. Retaining the prefix would let a producer invent any
98	// Nats-Dlq- header and have it ride into the DLQ looking like the library's own.
99	// The narrower rule does not make the VALUES unforgeable — a producer can still
100	// set Nats-Dlq-Origin-Subject on a message it publishes, and no header-level rule
101	// can tell that from a previous hop's writing — so read origin headers as "what
102	// the capture chain reported", not as something this package vouches for. What the
103	// list does buy is that the SHAPE is fixed: only these keys exist, only the per-hop
104	// ones are freshly authored, and an unknown Nats-Dlq- header never appears.
105	var dlqCarriedProvenance = []string{
106		DLQOriginRecordedHeader,
107		DLQOriginHeader,
108		DLQStreamSeqHeader,
109		DLQOriginStreamHeader,
110		DLQOriginDomainHeader,
111		DLQOriginTimestampHeader,

115	// natsHeaderPrefix is NATS's reserved header namespace. Everything the broker
116	// interprets lives under it, which is what makes it the right boundary to filter
117	// on — see the header policy on [DeadLetter].
118	const natsHeaderPrefix = "Nats-"

120	// keepsHeaderOnCapture reports whether a header from the original belongs on the
121	// captured copy.
122	//
123	// The rule is a namespace boundary, deliberately, and it is the third design of
124	// this filter. The first copied everything; the second named the directives to
125	// drop. Both failed the same way: a deny-list has to be complete against a set
126	// the broker keeps growing, and each round of "one more header" was a live
127	// silent-failure path in the meantime — expectations (err 10060), per-message TTL
128	// (10166), counter increments (10168), atomic-batch publishes (10174), each one
129	// able to fail a capture on every delivery and strand a message the DLQ would
130	// have taken.
131	//
132	// So this fails closed instead. Nats- is NATS's reserved header namespace: an
133	// application has no business writing there, and everything the broker
134	// interprets lives under it. A captured copy therefore keeps every header
135	// OUTSIDE that namespace verbatim — tracing (traceparent), application metadata,
136	// anything the payload's own readers rely on — and nothing at all from inside it.
137	//
138	// A directive NATS adds in a future release is dropped by this rule before anyone
139	// here has heard of it, which is the property the two earlier designs lacked. The
140	// matching is case-insensitive even though the broker's own lookup is a
141	// case-sensitive byte compare (server.getHeaderKeyIndex), so an oddly-cased
142	// directive is inert today: the cost of being stricter than necessary is nothing,
143	// and it holds if that ever changes.
144	//
145	// Nothing inside the namespace passes this filter, including this package's own
146	// [DLQHeaderPrefix]: a Nats-Dlq- header is not kept because it carries the prefix.
147	// The specific origin headers in [dlqCarriedProvenance] are then carried forward
148	// deliberately, by name, on top of the filtered copy — so an invented Nats-Dlq-
149	// field never rides through, and only the closed set this package defines exists on
150	// a captured copy.
151	//
152	// Also given up deliberately: the server-set republish and direct-get provenance
153	// (Nats-Stream, Nats-Sequence, Nats-Time-Stamp, Nats-Subject) on a message that
154	// was itself republished. Keeping those would mean asserting they are safe for a
155	// client to publish, which the client library explicitly says they are not. What
156	// matters about the captured message is re-stated in this package's own namespace,
157	// where the authorship is known.
158	func keepsHeaderOnCapture(key string) bool {
159		return !hasPrefixFold(key, natsHeaderPrefix)
160	}
161	
162	// hasPrefixFold is strings.HasPrefix under ASCII case folding. Header keys are
163	// ASCII by protocol, so a byte-wise fold is the whole of it.
164	func hasPrefixFold(s, prefix string) bool {
165		return len(s) >= len(prefix) && strings.EqualFold(s[:len(prefix)], prefix)
166	}

168	// dlqHops is how many captures the message being captured has already been
169	// through, from [DLQHopsHeader]. An absent or unparseable value reads as zero, so
170	// the next capture writes 1: a garbled count is worth less than a wrong one is
171	// harmful, and this field is reported rather than vouched for like the rest.
172	func dlqHops(src nats.Header) int {
173		n, err := strconv.Atoi(src.Get(DLQHopsHeader))
174		if err != nil || n < 0 {
175			return 0
176		}
177		return n
178	}

180	// Capture does not dedupe, and that is a decision rather than an omission.
181	//
182	// A captured copy goes to the DLQ with NO Nats-Msg-Id, so the broker stores every
183	// publish. The dedupe that used to be here existed for one narrow case: when the
184	// DLQ publish succeeds but the original's Ack does not, the message redelivers and
185	// is captured again, and a stable key let the duplicate window collapse the second
186	// copy onto the first.
187	//
188	// Every identity that can be synthesized for that has a collision class, and each
189	// one found so far was found in review rather than by reasoning ahead. The
190	// publisher's own Nats-Msg-Id collapses distinct originals, because JetStream
191	// dedupes on it stream-wide across every subject in the DLQ. Origin stream and
192	// sequence collapse across a stream that was deleted and recreated, since
193	// sequences restart. Adding the domain and the store timestamp closes those two —
194	// and the next scheme would meet the next broker behaviour the same way.
195	//
196	// The requirement is what gives, because the two failure directions are not
197	// comparable. A capture that stores a second copy is VISIBLE: a duplicate in a DLQ
198	// is a record someone can read, reconcile and discard, and at-least-once delivery
199	// already puts duplicates everywhere else in JetStream. A capture suppressed by a
200	// key collision is INVISIBLE: the broker answers with a successful PubAck marked
201	// Duplicate, the caller reads success and Acks the original, and the message is
202	// gone with no record — defeating the one guarantee this whole path exists to
203	// provide. So capture chooses its error direction the way the breaker's clock does
204	// (late, never early): duplicate, never suppressed.
205	//
206	// The cost is an occasional extra record in the failed-Ack window, bounded by the
207	// deliveries left on the ladder. Whoever replays can dedupe with far more context
208	// than a publish-time key affords, keying on the origin provenance above —
209	// [DLQOriginStreamHeader], [DLQStreamSeqHeader], [DLQOriginDomainHeader] and
210	// [DLQOriginTimestampHeader] identify the stored message the copy was made from.
211	
212	// DLQPublisher is the publish surface DeadLetter needs — the modern
213	// [JetStream] publish primitive (satisfied by jetstream.JetStream), aliased
214	// so DeadLetter's signature reads in DLQ terms. Kept minimal so wiring can
215	// hand it the same JetStream handle the per-cell publishers already hold,
216	// and tests can stub it.
217	type DLQPublisher = JetStream
218	
219	// SubjectToken sanitizes s into a single valid NATS subject token. NATS tokens
220	// cannot contain spaces, dots, or wildcards, so every character outside
221	// [a-z0-9_-] is replaced with '_' (and letters are lowercased). Use it to turn a
222	// human-readable dead-letter reason ("bad completion payload") into a subject
223	// token ("bad_completion_payload") — publishing to an unsanitized reason would
224	// fail, so the caller would never Ack the poison off a WorkQueue.
225	func SubjectToken(s string) string {
226		// Iterate bytes, not runes: we only keep ASCII [a-z0-9_-] and map everything
227		// else (including every byte of a multi-byte rune) to '_', so a byte loop is
228		// both correct and free of a rune->byte narrowing conversion.
229		b := make([]byte, 0, len(s))
230		for i := range len(s) {
231			c := s[i]
232			switch {
233			case c >= 'a' && c <= 'z', c >= '0' && c <= '9', c == '_', c == '-':
234				b = append(b, c)
235			case c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z':
236				b = append(b, c-'A'+'a')
237			default:
238				b = append(b, '_')
239			}
240		}
241		if len(b) == 0 {
242			return "unknown"
243		}
244		return string(b)
245	}
246	
247	// DeadLetter republishes a poison message to dlqSubject, preserving its payload
248	// and headers and adding Nats-Dlq-* provenance (reason, origin subject, origin
249	// stream, delivery count, stream sequence, and the original's own Nats-Msg-Id).
250	//
251	// "Headers" there means the ones an application owns. NATS's reserved Nats-
252	// namespace does not survive the copy — those are directives to the broker, and on
253	// the DLQ they would be obeyed against the wrong stream — and provenance is put
254	// back on top afterwards. See [keepsHeaderOnCapture] for the boundary and why it is
255	// a namespace rule rather than a list.
256	//
257	// The copy carries NO Nats-Msg-Id, so capture never dedupes; see the note above
258	// [DLQPublisher] for why that is deliberate and what it costs.
259	//
260	// # Write-once origin, fresh per-hop
261	//
262	// Capturing the same message twice must not lose what the first capture recorded.
263	// That happens for an ordinary reason: when the DLQ publish succeeds but the
264	// original's Ack does not, the message redelivers and is captured again. It also
265	// happens when a replay tool gives up on a DLQ record and dead-letters that.
266	//
267	// So the origin headers ([dlqCarriedProvenance]) are WRITE-ONCE: a value already on
268	// the message is carried through untouched, and only an absent one is filled in
269	// from the message being captured. First-hop identity — publisher's Nats-Msg-Id,
270	// origin subject, and the stream, sequence, domain and store time it was first
271	// stored at — therefore survives any number of hops without needing intermediate
272	// records to still exist. Per-hop fields are the opposite: reason and delivery
273	// count describe the capture that just happened and are written fresh, with
274	// [DLQHopsHeader] counting how many captures a record has been through.
275	//
276	// One limit, stated rather than implied: no header-level rule can distinguish an
277	// origin header written by an earlier hop from one a producer set on a message it
278	// published. Origin headers are what the capture chain REPORTED. What this package
279	// guarantees is the shape — only its own keys appear, per-hop fields are always its
280	// own, and an invented Nats-Dlq- field never survives.
281	//
282	// It is the capture step a consumer runs before giving up on a message it can
283	// never process. DeadLetter copies the poison to a durable DLQ subject so it can
284	// be inspected or replayed, and the caller then removes the original from the
285	// stream — a Term on the final delivery (see backoff.Policy.TermOnExhaustion,
286	// whose doc notes callers "DLQ capture before calling NakOrTerm") or a plain
287	// Ack. Without this step a Term'd or MaxDeliver-exhausted message is discarded
288	// with no trail; DeadLetter is what makes the give-up auditable and recoverable.
289	//
290	// Returns an error if the republish fails; on error the caller MUST NOT remove
291	// the original — Nak or leave it so the poison is never dropped without a
292	// captured copy. Publishing is bounded by dlqPublishTimeout regardless of ctx's
293	// deadline.
294	func DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, pub DLQPublisher, dlqSubject string, msg jetstream.Msg, reason string) error {
295		src := msg.Headers()
296		hdr := nats.Header{}
297		for k, v := range src {
298			// Filter on the way in rather than deleting afterwards: a copy that never
299			// holds a directive cannot leak one through a name this package failed to
300			// enumerate. See keepsHeaderOnCapture.
301			if !keepsHeaderOnCapture(k) {
302				continue
303			}
304			hdr[k] = append([]string(nil), v...)
305		}
306		meta, metaErr := msg.Metadata()
307		if metaErr != nil {
308			meta = nil
309		}
310	
311		// The origin block is written once, as a block, and afterwards only carried.
312		// Deciding that from [DLQOriginRecordedHeader] rather than from whether each
313		// field looks empty is what keeps a later hop from answering a question an
314		// earlier one already answered with "nothing" — see that header.
315		if src.Get(DLQOriginRecordedHeader) != "" {
316			// The namespace filter dropped these with the rest of Nats-; put back
317			// exactly the closed set and nothing else, absences included.
318			for _, h := range dlqCarriedProvenance {
319				if v := src.Get(h); v != "" {
320					hdr.Set(h, v)
321				}
322			}
323		} else {
324			hdr.Set(DLQOriginRecordedHeader, "1")
325			record := func(h, v string) {
326				if v != "" {
327					hdr.Set(h, v)
328				}
329			}
330			record(DLQOriginHeader, msg.Subject())
331			record(DLQOriginMsgIDHeader, src.Get(jetstream.MsgIDHeader))
332			if meta != nil {
333				record(DLQStreamSeqHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.Sequence.Stream, 10))
334				record(DLQOriginStreamHeader, meta.Stream)
335				// Empty outside a JetStream domain, and left absent when it is: the
336				// marker above already says the block was recorded, so absent reads as
337				// "no domain" rather than "ask the next hop".
338				record(DLQOriginDomainHeader, meta.Domain)
339				if !meta.Timestamp.IsZero() {
340					record(DLQOriginTimestampHeader, meta.Timestamp.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano))
341				}
342			}
343		}
344	
345		// Per-hop: always this capture's own.
346		hdr.Set(DLQReasonHeader, reason)
347		hdr.Set(DLQHopsHeader, strconv.Itoa(dlqHops(src)+1))
348		if meta != nil {
349			hdr.Set(DLQDeliveredHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.NumDelivered, 10))
350		}
351	
352		out := &nats.Msg{Subject: dlqSubject, Data: msg.Data(), Header: hdr}
353	
354		pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)
355		defer cancel()
356		if _, err := pub.PublishMsg(pubCtx, out); err != nil {
357			return fmt.Errorf("dead-letter publish to %q: %w", dlqSubject, err)
358		}
359		return nil
360	}

# COR-1487 — DeadLetter must survive a cancelled caller context

## Context

`natsmsg.DeadLetter` is the give-up capture a consumer runs *before* dropping a poison
message. It bounds its publish with:

```go
pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)   // deadletter.go:354
```

`context.WithTimeout` caps the deadline **and inherits the parent's cancellation**. The
jobs most likely to need dead-lettering are exactly the ones whose ctx is already dead
(SIGTERM, a cancelled upstream call), so the publish context is born dead: `PublishMsg`
fails with `context canceled` before touching the network and the 15s bound never
applies. Confirmed in staging and prod logs.

The function's own doc already promises the fixed behaviour ("Publishing is bounded by
`dlqPublishTimeout` regardless of ctx's deadline") — the original reasoning considered
only whether ctx carried a *deadline*, and missed that it can still be *cancelled*. So
this is a bugfix restoring the documented contract, shipping as a patch release.

`ctx` is used for exactly one thing in `DeadLetter`: `pub.PublishMsg(pubCtx, out)`.

**Repo/branch:** `/Users/georgf/src/entireio/go-nuts`, base `main @ befb4d7` (clean, in
sync with origin). Work branch: `georg/cor-1487-deadletter-withoutcancel`.

**Hard stops:** do NOT run `entire session attach`; do NOT open/merge the PR or tag
`v0.9.2`. Finish at a pushed branch.

## Prior art found during exploration

`jsconsumer/retry.go:1037` already does the equivalent detach one layer up
(`settleCtx := context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`), with a long comment explaining the
ShutdownGroup interaction — this fix is the same reasoning applied at the natsmsg layer.
`jsconsumer/retry_test.go:1022` has `ctxRespectingDLQ`, a fake that fails a publish on a
cancelled ctx and records what it saw, plus
`TestTerminateSurvivesAShutdownCancelledContext` (line 1067). The new natsmsg test is the
missing lower layer of exactly that pattern, and should mirror its shape and comment
voice.

## 1. The fix — `natsmsg/deadletter.go:354`

Replace the `context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)` line with:

```go
	// WithoutCancel, not the bare ctx: the capture must outlive a cancelled job.
	// The jobs most likely to need dead-lettering are exactly the ones whose ctx
	// is already dead (SIGTERM, a cancelled upstream call), and WithTimeout
	// inherits cancellation as well as capping the deadline — so the bare ctx
	// produced a publish context born dead and the bound below never applied
	// (COR-1487). Values are preserved, so the handler's span still carries.
	pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), dlqPublishTimeout)
```

## 2. `DeadLetter`'s doc comment — last paragraph (`deadletter.go:292-293`)

Replace "Publishing is bounded by dlqPublishTimeout regardless of ctx's deadline." with
wording that says **cancellation** explicitly (the old "deadline"-only phrasing is how
the gap survived review): the publish is detached from ctx's cancellation and bounded by
`dlqPublishTimeout`; ctx's values still propagate, so a handler's span carries into the
capture. Cite COR-1487.

## 3. `dlqPublishTimeout`'s doc (`deadletter.go:14-19`) — record the shutdown interaction

Add a sentence: `nuts.DefaultJoinTimeout` is 10s (`shutdown.go:17`) while this bound is
15s, and `ShutdownGroup` cancels the loops, joins, then drains the connections — so a
capture racing shutdown gets ~10s before the connection is drained under it and fails
with a connection error. Detaching narrows that window rather than closing it. **Neither
value changes**; this is written down so it isn't rediscovered.

## 4. Leave alone — deliberately

Verified this is the complete `context.WithTimeout` inventory outside test code:

- `natsmsg/publish.go:116` (`Publisher.Publish`) — same shape, but inheriting
  cancellation is CORRECT there: an ordinary producer wants to abandon and fall back to
  its outbox/nak/5xx path. Not a give-up capture. **Untouched.**
- `jsconsumer/retry.go:1037` — `settleCtx` becomes redundant for the capture but MUST
  STAY: it also feeds the DoubleAck bound (`context.WithTimeout(settleCtx, dlqAckTimeout)`
  at line 1067), which this fix does not cover. Removing it re-exposes the ack.
  **Only change: one sentence added to the existing comment** noting the capture is now
  detached inside `natsmsg.DeadLetter` too, and that `settleCtx` remains load-bearing for
  the DoubleAck — so a future reader does not "simplify" it away.
- `jsconsumer/floor.go:275` — liveness poll during normal operation; inheriting
  cancellation is right. **Untouched.**

## 5. The test — `natsmsg/deadletter_test.go`

**The fake must be made discriminating first.** `fakeDLQPublisher.PublishMsg`
(line 44) takes `_ context.Context` and ignores ctx entirely, so a cancellation test
written against it today would pass against the *unfixed* code. All 12 existing
`DeadLetter` call sites in this file pass `context.Background()`, so binding ctx is inert
for them.

**(a) Bind ctx in the fake** (`deadletter_test.go:33-69`) — add fields and a ctx check,
in the fake's own stated voice ("a fake that ignores expectations cannot fail the way the
broker does"):

```go
type fakeDLQPublisher struct {
	msgs      []*nats.Msg
	seenIDs   map[string]bool
	err       error
	deadlines []time.Time // per publish; zero when the ctx carried none
	probes    []any       // per publish: ctx.Value(dlqProbeKey{})
}

// dlqProbeKey is how a test plants a value on the caller's context and reads it
// back from inside the publish — the property WithoutCancel preserves and a
// bare context.Background() would silently lose.
type dlqProbeKey struct{}
```

still records what it saw):

```go
	d, _ := ctx.Deadline()
	f.deadlines = append(f.deadlines, d)
	f.probes = append(f.probes, ctx.Value(dlqProbeKey{}))
	// A real client fails before the wire on a dead context. Without this the
	// cancellation test below passes just as happily on the broken code.
	if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
```

expectations paragraph.

1. with an already-cancelled parent, `DeadLetter` returns nil and the fake captured
   exactly 1 message;
2. the ctx the fake saw still carries a deadline ~`dlqPublishTimeout` (15s) out — the
   bound must survive, that is half the ticket. Bracket it against `time.Now()` taken
   immediately before and after the call rather than asserting a loose "remaining >

```go
	parent := context.WithValue(t.Context(), dlqProbeKey{}, "trace-1")
	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)
	cancel() // exactly the state shutdown leaves: ctx dead, connection still up
```

Declare the expected bound as a local `const` in the test with a comment that it mirrors
the unexported `dlqPublishTimeout` (the test file is `package natsmsg_test` and cannot
reference it).

1. `go test ./natsmsg/ -run TestDeadLetterCapturesWithAnAlreadyCancelledParent` → PASS

3. re-run → must FAIL
4. restore the fix, re-run → PASS

failure output.

From the repo root, all three must be clean:

- `mise run build`
- `mise run lint` (golangci-lint 2.11.4, `.golangci.yaml`: `wrapcheck`, `revive`,
  `usetesting`, `errorlint` among ~60 linters)
- `mise run test:ci` (`go test -race ./...`, includes the embedded real-broker
  `internal/brokersemantics` suite, which calls `natsmsg.DeadLetter` with a live

Plus the mutation-verify loop in 5(c) as the actual proof the test bites.

## 7. Hand-off

Branch `georg/cor-1487-deadletter-withoutcancel` off `main`, one commit in house style

`natsmsg.DeadLetter` is the give-up capture a consumer runs *before* dropping a poison
message. It bounds its publish with:

```go
pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)   // deadletter.go:354
```

`context.WithTimeout` caps the deadline **and inherits the parent's cancellation**. The
jobs most likely to need dead-lettering are exactly the ones whose ctx is already dead
(SIGTERM, a cancelled upstream call), so the publish context is born dead: `PublishMsg`
fails with `context canceled` before touching the network and the 15s bound never
applies. Confirmed in staging and prod logs.

The function's own doc already promises the fixed behaviour ("Publishing is bounded by
`dlqPublishTimeout` regardless of ctx's deadline") — the original reasoning considered
only whether ctx carried a *deadline*, and missed that it can still be *cancelled*. So
this is a bugfix restoring the documented contract, shipping as a patch release.

`ctx` is used for exactly one thing in `DeadLetter`: `pub.PublishMsg(pubCtx, out)`.

**Repo/branch:** `/Users/georgf/src/entireio/go-nuts`, base `main @ befb4d7` (clean, in

natsmsg: detach the dead-letter capture from the caller's cancellation (COR-1487)

DeadLetter bounded its publish with context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout),
which caps the deadline AND inherits the parent's cancellation. It is the
give-up capture a consumer runs before dropping a poison message, so the jobs
most likely to reach it are exactly the ones whose ctx is already dead — a
SIGTERM landing mid-handler, a cancelled upstream call. The publish context was
born dead: PublishMsg failed with context.Canceled before touching the network
and the 15s bound never applied. Seen in staging and prod.

dlqPublishTimeout regardless of ctx's deadline"); the reasoning behind it
considered only whether ctx carried a deadline and missed that it can still be
cancelled. So this restores a documented contract rather than changing one, and
the doc now says cancellation explicitly — along with the cost, which is that
against an unreachable broker the call blocks for the bound instead of failing
at once, and a capture racing shutdown can outlast the join window.

ctx's values still propagate, so the handler's span carries into the capture.

real-broker one. The shared fakeDLQPublisher now refuses a dead context the way
a real client does — until now it ignored ctx entirely, so a cancellation test
written against it would have passed against the broken code.

Publisher.Publish keeps inheriting cancellation (a producer wants to abandon and
fall back to its outbox/nak/5xx path), and jsconsumer's settleCtx stays because
it is what detaches the DoubleAck, which this does not cover.

## Fixed (6)

| Finding | Change |
|---|---|
| `dlqPublishTimeout` doc did arithmetic over a **tunable** default — "`DefaultJoinTimeout` is 10s … therefore ~10s" is wrong for anyone using `nuts.WithJoinTimeout`, and rots if the default moves | Now states the *relation* (whenever the join window is shorter, the drain cuts the capture short), with the numbers marked as defaults and the override named |
| The inline comment at the fix restated three facts already in the doc comment ~70 lines above | Trimmed to the one fact the doc doesn't carry — that `WithTimeout` inherits cancellation as well as capping — plus a pointer up |
| `ctxRecordingDLQ` used two parallel append-only slices for a call that publishes exactly once | Collapsed to scalars `deadline`/`probe`, matching `ctxRecordingMsg`'s style in `jsconsumer/retry_test.go` |
| `dlqProbeKey`'s doc and the assertion comment stated the same "why not `Background()`" sentence twice | Key doc says what it keys; the reasoning stays at the check that turns on it |
| My `retry.go` sentence argued "redundant, but don't delete" — the weakest available framing, and an invitation to the deletion it warned against | Flipped to the positive: the *whole settle sequence* runs detached, and this is what covers the DoubleAck |
| My local `const payload` silenced `goconst` by dropping one occurrence below the threshold, leaving two bare literals in the same file | Hoisted to a package-level `poisonPayload` used at all three comparison sites (verified: the linter was reporting against the *sibling* test, not mine) |

## Skipped (5)

- **Delete `settleCtx`, detach at the DoubleAck call site instead** (altitude + simplification both proposed it) — you ruled it MUST STAY and we re-confirmed that in review. Both agents conceded defence-in-depth is a real counter-argument.
- **Export `DefaultDeadLetterTimeout`** — new exported API turns a patch into a minor. Real gap though: the doc says "blocks for `dlqPublishTimeout`", a symbol external callers can't resolve, and my test has to hardcode 15s. Worth a follow-up ticket.
- **`storedMsg` / `fetchOne` harness helpers** — the DLQ read-back is hand-rolled 9× and `fetchAll`+length-check 10× across `internal/brokersemantics`. Genuine, but it's a package-wide refactor of pre-existing tests; burying it in a one-line bugfix is the wrong commit. Best follow-up of the three.
- **`deadline.IsZero()` is derivable from the bracket check** — kept: a zero time does fail the bracket, but "carried no deadline" is a far clearer failure than `0001-01-01 … outside [...]`.
- **Move the `publish.go` comment to godoc** — you decided inline deliberately, so the grep for `context.WithTimeout` lands on it.

Efficiency found nothing, and disproved two of my own premises: the new form is *faster* (`withoutCancelCtx.Done()` is nil, so `propagateCancel` never registers in the shared parent's children map — 4.6× better under contention), and the new broker test adds no measurable wall-clock.
